derivedFrom.none: a basic colour adjective (the measure أَفْعَل)

elative.none: a colour: whiter is أَشَدُّ بَيَاضًا (أَفْعَل is already the colour)

profile.feeling: Snow, milk, a white house in the sun.

examples.tr: The White House is in Washington.

collocations.tr: the Mediterranean Sea (“the white middle sea”)

synonyms.nuance: bright, snow-white — intensifies whiteness: أَبْيَضُ نَاصِعٌ

etymology.text: Wiktionary: a colour adjective (pattern أَفْعَل) from the root ب ي ض (b y ḍ).

funFacts: The Mediterranean is الْبَحْرُ الْأَبْيَضُ الْمُتَوَسِّطُ, “the white middle sea” — Turkish Akdeniz is also “the white sea”.
بَيْض (eggs, lesson 7) has the same root ب ي ض: the egg is “the white one”.
pitfalls: A colour of the pattern أَفْعَل is a diptote (no tanwīn): قَمِيصٌ أَبْيَضُ (a white shirt), not *أَبْيَضٌ; feminine بَيْضَاء, plural بِيض.
The feminine has another shape: سَيَّارَةٌ بَيْضَاءُ, not *أَبْيَضَة.
subtleties: “Whiter” is not *أَبْيَضُ مِنْ: Wiktionary gives أَشَدُّ بَيَاضًا or أَنْصَعُ بَيَاضًا (“stronger in whiteness”).

derivedFrom.none: a basic colour adjective (the measure أَفْعَل)

elative.none: a colour: blacker is أَشَدُّ سَوَادًا

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

senses.def: dark, gloomy (figurative): يَوْمٌ أَسْوَدُ, a black day

etymology.text: Wiktionary: a colour adjective (pattern أَفْعَل) from the root س و د (s w d).

funFacts: السُّودَان (Sudan) is one of its plurals: “the black (people)” — Wiktionary lists سُود and سُودَان.
The Black Sea is الْبَحْرُ الْأَسْوَدُ, like Turkish Karadeniz.
pitfalls: Diptote, feminine سَوْدَاءُ, plural سُود: حَقِيبَةٌ سَوْدَاءُ, a black bag.
Unvocalized اسود can also be أُسُود, “lions” (plural of أَسَد).
subtleties: سُوق (market) is feminine here: السُّوقُ السَّوْدَاءُ.

derivedFrom.none: a basic colour adjective (the measure أَفْعَل)

elative.none: a colour: redder is أَشَدُّ حُمْرَةً

profile.feeling: Tomatoes, roses, a red car — and anger.

examples.tr: The Red Sea is between Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: a colour adjective (pattern أَفْعَل) from the root ح م ر (ḥ m r).

funFacts: The Alhambra in Granada is الْحَمْرَاءُ, “the red (one)”.
pitfalls: Diptote, feminine حَمْرَاءُ, plural حُمْر: سَيَّارَةٌ حَمْرَاءُ (a red car), هٰذِهِ أَقْلَامٌ حَمْرَاءُ (these are red pens).
subtleties: “Redder” is أَكْثَرُ حُمْرَةً or أَشَدُّ حُمْرَةً (Wiktionary): colours of the pattern أَفْعَل have no elative of their own.

derivedFrom.none: a basic colour adjective (the measure أَفْعَل)

elative.none: a colour: bluer is أَشَدُّ زُرْقَةً

etymology.text: Wiktionary: a colour adjective (pattern أَفْعَل) from the root ز ر ق (z r q); its first sense is “flickering, glinting” — compare Ancient Greek γλαυκός (glaukós) for the same development.

funFacts: Greek γλαυκός also went from “gleaming” to “blue-grey” (Wiktionary compares them).
Zarqāʾ al-Yamāma, “the blue(-eyed) woman of al-Yamāma”, is a legendary Arabian woman who could see riders three days away.
pitfalls: Diptote, feminine زَرْقَاءُ, plural زُرْق: سَيَّارَةٌ زَرْقَاءُ.
subtleties: Light and dark shades follow the colour: أَزْرَقُ فَاتِحٌ, أَزْرَقُ غَامِقٌ.

derivedFrom.none: a basic colour adjective (the measure أَفْعَل)

elative.none: a colour: greener is أَشَدُّ خُضْرَةً

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

examples.tr: The park is green in spring.

examples.text: قَدْ يَعْنِي الْأَخْضَرُ فِي الشِّعْرِ الْقَدِيمِ الْأَسْوَدَ أَوِ الدَّاكِنَ.
examples.tr: In old poetry al-aḫḍar can mean black or dark.

examples.text: مَا أَظَلَّتِ الْخَضْرَاءُ وَلَا أَقَلَّتِ الْغَبْرَاءُ أَصْدَقَ مِنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ.
examples.tr: Neither has the dark one (the sky) shaded nor the dusty one (the earth) carried anyone more truthful than Abū Ḏarr (hadith).

etymology.text: Wiktionary: a colour adjective (pattern أَفْعَل) from the root خ ض ر (ḫ ḍ r).

funFacts: خُضَار (vegetables, “the greens”) has the same root خ ض ر.
pitfalls: Diptote, feminine خَضْرَاءُ, plural خُضْر: الْحَدِيقَةُ خَضْرَاءُ.
subtleties: To give the green light = أَعْطَى الضَّوْءَ الْأَخْضَرَ, as in English.

elative.none: a colour: yellower is أَشَدُّ صُفْرَةً

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

etymology.text: Wiktionary: a colour adjective (pattern أَفْعَل) from the root ص ف ر (ṣ f r).

funFacts: صِفْر (zero, lesson 5) is written with the same root letters ص ف ر; Arabic صِفْر, “empty”, gave European cipher and zero.
pitfalls: Diptote, feminine صَفْرَاءُ, plural صُفْر: الْبِطَاقَةُ الصَّفْرَاءُ.
subtleties: A pale, sick face is “yellow” in Arabic: وَجْهُهُ أَصْفَرُ.

elative.none: a colour in -ī: compared with أَغْمَقُ / أَفْتَحُ (darker / lighter) or أَكْثَرُ

synonyms.nuance: brown, dark — of skin and hair (tanned, brunette); feminine سَمْرَاء

etymology.text: Wiktionary: from بُنّ (bunn, “coffee beans”) + the adjective ending ـِيّ (-iyy) — “coffee-coloured”; بُنّ is borrowed from Classical Syriac.

funFacts: Literally “coffee-bean coloured”: بُنّ is the coffee bean.
pitfalls: A nisba adjective in -iyy: fully regular, with tanwīn — بُنِّيٌّ, بُنِّيَّةٌ (unlike أَحْمَرُ, حَمْرَاءُ).
For skin and hair Arabic says أَسْمَر, not بُنِّيّ.
subtleties: Things in the plural agree in the feminine singular: عُيُونُهُ بُنِّيَّةٌ (his eyes are brown).

synonyms.nuance: lead-grey (from رَصَاص, lead) — common in speech

funFacts: “Ash-coloured”, like Greek σταχτής / σταχτί (from στάχτη, ash) and Russian пепельный.
pitfalls: A nisba adjective: regular, with tanwīn — رَمَادِيٌّ, رَمَادِيَّةٌ.
subtleties: Grey hair from age is also شَعْرٌ أَشْيَبُ (from شَيْب, grey hair).

profile.synonymsNone: No other word in standard Arabic; some dialects say بُرْتُقَانِي.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: بُرْتُقَال (burtuqāl, “orange (fruit)”) + ـِيّ (-iyy); بُرْتُقَال is borrowed from Ottoman Turkish portokal, or more likely from Greek πορτοκάλι, and is a doublet of الْبُرْتُغَال, Portugal.

funFacts: Greek πορτοκάλι, Turkish portakal, Arabic بُرْتُقَال: the sweet orange is “the Portugal fruit”.
pitfalls: A nisba adjective: regular, with tanwīn — بُرْتُقَالِيٌّ, بُرْتُقَالِيَّةٌ.
subtleties: The fruit is بُرْتُقَال (a collective noun), the colour بُرْتُقَالِيّ.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses وَرْدِيّ “rose, roseate; of a reddish or purplish tint that resembles the color of roses” — the colour pink, the course concept.

examples.tr: My daughter loves the colour pink.

synonyms.nuance: pink (“flower-coloured”) — the everyday word in the Levant

etymology.text: Wiktionary: from وَرْد (ward, “roses, blossoms”) + ـِيّ (-iyy); وَرْد, like Hebrew וֶרֶד and Ancient Greek ῥόδον, is borrowed from a reflex of Proto-Iranian *wardah.

funFacts: Rose = وَرْد, Hebrew וֶרֶד (vered), Greek ρόδο: one Iranian word behind all three (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: A nisba adjective: regular, with tanwīn — وَرْدِيٌّ, وَرْدِيَّةٌ.
subtleties: As in English, “rosy” can mean hopeful: أَحْلَامٌ وَرْدِيَّةٌ.

root.none: made from بَنَفْسَج (violet), a loanword from Persian

pattern.none: a nisba made from a loanword: no measure of its own

elative.none: a colour in -ī: compared with أَغْمَقُ / أَفْتَحُ (darker / lighter) or أَكْثَرُ

etymology.text: Wiktionary: بَنَفْسَج (banafsaj, “violet” — the flower) + ـِيّ (-iyy); بَنَفْسَج comes from Middle Iranian (compare Persian بنفشه, banafše).

funFacts: The same Persian flower name is Turkish menekşe and Greek μενεξές (violet).
pitfalls: A nisba adjective: regular, with tanwīn — بَنَفْسَجِيٌّ, بَنَفْسَجِيَّةٌ.
subtleties: “Ultraviolet” is literally “above the violet”: فَوْقَ الْبَنَفْسَجِيِّ.

features.derivedFrom: the active participle of فَتَحَ (to open)

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

examples.tr: Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror took Constantinople.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: derived from the active participle of فَتَحَ (fataḥa, “to open, to conquer”) — an “opening” colour.

funFacts: Istanbul’s Fatih district and Fatih Sultan Mehmet carry its other sense: الْفَاتِح, “the Conqueror”.
pitfalls: It goes after the colour word: أَزْرَقُ فَاتِحٌ (light blue). With a feminine noun, the safe way is to speak about the colour (لَوْن, masculine): لَوْنُ السَّيَّارَةِ أَزْرَقُ فَاتِحٌ.
subtleties: Not “light” in weight (خَفِيف) and not “light” as in bright (مُضِيء).

features.derivedFrom: the active participle of غَمُقَ (to be dark)

examples.tr: I like dark colours in winter.
The car’s colour is dark blue.

synonyms.nuance: dark — the written word, also of skin and clouds

etymology.text: Wiktionary: derived from the active participle of غَمُقَ (ġamuqa); elative أَغْمَق.

funFacts: Standard writing often prefers دَاكِن; in speech غَامِق is the usual word.
pitfalls: Only for colours: a dark room is غُرْفَةٌ مُظْلِمَةٌ, not *غَامِقَةٌ.
subtleties: It follows the colour word, like فَاتِح: أَخْضَرُ غَامِقٌ.

feminine.none: an elative: one form for both genders in comparisons (هِيَ أَكْثَرُ …); the feminine كُثْرَى is rare

plurals.none: an elative: one form (أَكْثَرُ) for every number and gender in comparisons

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: Quantity and preference: more than, most of, the most.

senses.def: most, the most; most of: أَكْثَرُ النَّاسِ, الْأَكْثَرُ

examples.tr: I like tea more than coffee.
My brother eats more than me.
This is the most visited city.

synonyms.nuance: most of, the greater part — before a definite noun: مُعْظَمُ النَّاسِ
more (of something): الْمَزِيدُ مِنَ الْمَاءِ, more water

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the elative of كَثِير (kaṯīr, “much, many”), of the root ك ث ر.

funFacts: Where Greek and Turkish add a word (πιο, daha), Arabic usually makes a new word: كَبِير → أَكْبَر. أَكْثَر is the elative of كَثِير — “more” is literally “much-er”.
pitfalls: Not for adjectives that have an elative: bigger is أَكْبَرُ, not *أَكْثَرُ كَبِيرًا.
For colours and many participles it is the only way: أَكْثَرُ + a noun in the accusative — أَكْثَرُ تَعَبًا (more tired).
subtleties: After a verb, “more” is accusative: أُحِبُّ الشَّايَ أَكْثَرَ.
أَكْثَرُ + a definite plural = most of: أَكْثَرُ الطُّلَّابِ.
